content: The BPAL regimen, which consists of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, was evaluated across seven categories, including patient-friendliness and treatment safety monitoring. It demonstrated higher acceptability compared to longer MDR-TB treatment regimens in six of the seven categories. The exception was treatment safety monitoring, where the difference was negligible. The overall likelihood of implementing BPAL as a standard of care for XDR-TB and MDR-TB treatment failure or intolerance was rated at 88, with only 1% of participants deeming it unlikely and 11% expressing a neutral opinion. For MDR-TB patients with fluoroquinolone resistance, the likelihood of implementation was similarly high at 84%, regardless of additional resistance to second-line injectables. This suggests feasibility from the perspective of interviewed stakeholders. The Nix-TB study, conducted by the TB Alliance, was a phase III, open-label, prospective cohort study assessing the safety, efficacy, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of a 6-month BPAL regimen, extendable to 9 months if necessary. The study enrolled patients aged 14 years or older with confirmed XDR-TB or MDR/RR-TB who could not tolerate or did not respond to previous treatments. Patients were followed for up to 24 months post-treatment. Secondary outcomes included bacteriological failure or relapse, time to sputum culture conversion, and changes in TB symptoms and health status. The regimen included pretomanid (200 mg/day), bedaquiline (400 mg/day for 2 weeks, then 200 mg three times weekly), and linezolid (initially 1200 mg/day, with adjustments based on tolerability). The study revealed a high rate of adverse events related to the drugs, with 57% of participants experiencing at least one serious adverse event. Grade 3–4 adverse events included peripheral neuropathy, elevated hepatic transaminases, hematological issues, increased pancreatic enzymes, and optic neuritis. These events led to discontinuation of all three drugs in one participant and linezolid in 35 participants (32%). Only 17% completed the full course of linezolid at 1200 mg/day. The GDG noted challenges in comparing adverse event rates with other studies due to differences in reporting and assessment methods. Pretomanid demonstrated activity against replicating and non-replicating bacilli in a doseand concentration-dependent manner. However, preclinical data highlighted safety concerns, including liver toxicities and reproductive toxicities in animal models, some of which appeared irreversible. Pharmacokinetic modeling suggested that linezolid toxicity is dose-dependent, with anemia manageable through close monitoring and dose adjustments. Peripheral neuropathy, when it occurred, was reversible in most cases within three months. The GDG considered the BPAL regimen's shortened treatment duration and reduced drug exposure as desirable effects, despite the high rate of adverse events. However, direct comparisons with newer all-oral longer regimens recommended by WHO in 2019 were not possible due to a lack of available outcome data. The GDG emphasized the need for further research and monitoring to address safety concerns and optimize dosing strategies.
